title: The hard part of dementia care isn't the patient — it's the caregiver who gets ground down
dek: The hard part of dementia care isn't the illness itself but the caregiver worn down day after day — caregiving turns a wife into a nurse, forces a millennial to quit her job; love is the starting point but not the support, and the system has yet to catch these families.
why: This is not senior-wellness popular science but a sociologist's field honesty after walking into dementia households: no standard answers, only a reality you must see in advance.
who: Urban only children born in the 80s and 90s, and anyone whose parents are starting to age while they have made no eldercare arrangements at all; also for those who want to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care gap ends up pressed back onto every family
points.body: China has 323 million people over 60, 23% of the population; 35 million are disabled elders, but there are only about 500,000 eldercare workers. The supply gap has not been absorbed by the market or institutions, and the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China's patient count is nearly 30% of the world's, and the host estimates that on average one in every 20 Chinese families is affected — for the first generation of only children, this may be a reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms; the movies can't be trusted
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, the misunderstanding Tang Yong most wants to correct is this: there is no uniform image of a person with dementia. Society's imagination of dementia mostly comes from films, neighbors or hearsay; the professor's incontinence in Still Alice is only one form. He has met a tailor who, after dementia set in, still noticed stains on a visitor's clothes and taught people to remove them with orange peel; and a man disabled by a car accident who, when he could only hum Liuyang River, wore an expression of total focus. Dementia itself covers Alzheimer's, vascular dementia and other causes; each person's life imprint lingers in a different way, and caregiving cannot be performed from a script.

points.h: The dementia village ideal is paid for by state nursing insurance
points.body: Most people take the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: elders here stroll the supermarket and visit the café like residents, while staff play shopkeepers to keep up a normal atmosphere. But the details the host adds expose how hard it is to replicate — the 23 homes built in 2009 cost more than 18 million euros, of which 17.8 million was borne by the government, and residents' fees are also covered by long-term care-related systems. What Tang Yong saw in a low-income American nursing home was the opposite: elevators had to be locked to keep dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease, and the difference lies not in ideals but in the state's payment system.

points.h: Love isn't enough, and sacrifice will grind down the caregiver
points.body: The host sums up the caregiver's predicament precisely: many people swing back and forth between ‘I love my mom and dad so much’ and ‘I'm about to be crushed by my mom and dad’. Tang Yong says caregiving is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse has to learn to bathe, feed and handle emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by the relationship between nurse and patient. Long-term sacrifice is not a devotion to be romanticized: a daughter he interviewed in Guangzhou twenty years ago divorced and fell into severe depression after caring for her disabled father; the book also includes a millennial caregiver forced to quit her job by caregiving pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, the caregiver becomes a patient too.

points.h: The more you see, the less certain eldercare becomes
points.body: After years of researching elder care, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his parents' old age. He is a first-generation only child, his parents are both 75 this year, and the more cases he sees the less certain he feels; his research assistant even said after every interview that the more families she saw, the less she knew how she would arrange things for her own parents. Families with multiple children have friction too: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough caregiving gives the elder bedsores; only-child families lack manpower to share the load, and some who bring their parents to Shenzhen find rent, medical bills and nanny fees stacking up faster than pensions rise. An ideal model cannot be designed by a single child alone.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing something every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that the caregiver must repeatedly accept loss. Volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elder who at first could paint blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later only dared to praise others and not put brush to paper; another elder's husband reported a new loss every week: his wife could not recognize the great-grandchild his daughter had just borne, and did not know where this child had come from. This day-after-day, irreversible downward slide drains a caregiver more than physical disability. The length of caregiving is not the repetition of hardship but a small goodbye faced every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance is here, but it can't catch every elder
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016 and had spread to about 90 cities by around 2025, with the official pace set at universal coverage within the next two or three years. But Tang Yong cautions that long-term care insurance does not hand money to every elder; through unified assessment it mainly covers those with moderate to severe disability, paying for home nursing, meal delivery and other services; those with mild conditions may not qualify. The hardest part is mindset: putting parents in a nursing home is often equated with unfiliality in China, and elders feel like the grandfather in the interviews who said that after a month there his hair was nearly falling out. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the share who actively choose institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap will not disappear on its own.
